title: Analytics Projects
text:
What Should We Do Next?

Double down on High Value segment – they respond best and deliver positive ROI.
Re-engage Medium Value customers with tailored content (e.g., product recommendations).
Test a lighter touch for Low Value segment – maybe a single reminder email instead of a full campaign.
Improve open rates – since opens strongly predict response, A/B test subject lines and send times.

title: Analytics Projects
text:
Final Thought

“Not all customers are created equal. By focusing on segments that drive ROI, we can increase marketing efficiency and build stronger relationships.”

title: M04-Reflection Essay-Advanced Data Visualization
text:
1 Summarize what you learned from the presentation by Thomas Lin Pedersen on “ggplot2 workshop: Part 2 in Step 1
homas Lin Pedersen demonstrated that the grammar of graphics is not limited to static charts. By maintaining the core structure of data, aesthetics, geoms, and scales, we can build powerful extensions.
Two extensions stood out to me:

patchwork: Allows you to combine multiple plots into a single layout, making it easier to tell a cohesive story.
gganimate: Introduces time as a dimension, turning static data into a dynamic narrative.


# patchwork examples

library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)

# Create two simple plots
p1 <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(title = "Scatter Plot")

p2 <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = factor(cyl))) +
  geom_bar(fill = "steelblue") +
  labs(title = "Bar Plot", x = "Cylinders")

# Combine them side-by-side
p1 + p2








2 In Step 2, a short video on “ggplot2 Scales and Transformations - Data Communication / Data Visualization | Video (13:36)” was introduced. (1) Summarize it and (2) discuss how it fits with the grammar of graphics you learned in Step 1.
Scales act as the interpreter between your raw data and the visual elements on the plot. The video reinforced that scales control the mapping of data values to visual channels like position, color, and size.
Takeaways:

Modifying axis breaks, limits, and labels enhances clarity.
Transformations are crucial for visualizing skewed data.

Scales are the mechanism that refines the mapping defined in the aesthetic layer. While Step 1 taught us what to map, Step 2 taught us how to control the perception of that map.

3 In Step 3, David Robinson’s video demonstrates impromptu data visualization. List three new functions that were not taught previously but were deemed helpful for you in the future. Briefly explain what you can do with each of the functions
David Robinson’s exploratory analysis introduced me to three highly practical functions that improve readability and speed.






Function
Purpose



fct_reorder()
Reorders factor levels by a numeric value to make bar charts cleaner.


geom_smooth()
Adds a trend line (e.g., linear model or LOESS) to a scatter plot.


coord_flip()
Swaps the x and y axes, perfect for horizontal bar charts with long labels.



4 What did you like about the gt and gtExtra packages demonstrated in Step 4? How do they complement data visualization using charts that we have spent so much time on so far? Under what circumstances would you prefer to use tables over charts in visualization data?
While charts are excellent for spotting trends, tables are irreplaceable when precision is paramount. The gt package provides incredible control over table formatting, from font styling to grouping rows. The gtExtras package enhances this by embedding visualizations like sparklines directly into cells.
Scenarios where a table is better than chart;

Displaying exact regression outputs or financial summaries.
Situations where the user needs to look up specific values rather than compare shapes.
When space is limited and precise numbers are the primary message

5 Pick three tips and tricks you learned from Data Visualization guru Cédric Schere in Step 5 and explain why you liked them. 
Cédric Scherer emphasized that statistical accuracy must be paired with thoughtful design. His tips are about removing obstacles between the data and the viewer.

Use Thoughtful Color Schemes: Avoid default palettes. Use deliberate, limited colors to guide the viewer’s eye.
Direct Labeling: Place labels next to lines instead of relying on a separate legend. This reduces the cognitive load on the reader.
Embrace Minimalism: Remove unnecessary gridlines, backgrounds, and borders to let the data stand out.

6 In Step 6, you will find my advanced visualization notebook. Run the codes one by one and digest as much as you can. What are you most impressed with about the visualization approach or tools demonstrated in the codebook? 
The integration of multiple variables in single plots was the best feature that I liked in the advanced visualization notebook. The interactive bubble charts were used to show the possibility of displaying four or five variables at the same time without confusion. The animation also section was very strong in my view since it turned the stagnant images into moving stories as time progressed. The examples of the geospatial mapping demonstrated the effectiveness of overlaying the data onto the world and regional maps. The most impressive part to me was that each extra line of code was added to the chart and it was improved. This supported the stratified method of grammar instruction and proved the skills of higher order narrative.

7 What seems to be the challenge, if any, for you when you try to master data visualization skills? How may you be able to overcome the challenge?
My main challenge is balancing complexity with clarity. It is easy to add layers and extensions, but difficult to ensure the final product is accessible to the audience. Additionally, memorizing the vast number of ggplot2 arguments and extension functions is daunting. To overcome these I will adopt the following strategies;

Regular Practice: Recreate one published chart per week, trying to modify its style.
Build a Code Snippet Library: Save useful code patterns
Iterative Design: Follow the examples of Pedersen, Robinson, and Scherer by starting simple and adding complexity only when it serves the story.

title: M02-Introduction to Data Science in R-Reflection
text:
1 Summarize new things you learned in this module about reproducible data science and literate coding

Reproducible data science and literate coding showed me a promising path of integrating analysis, documentation, and transparency into a workflow unified. Literate programming enables researcher to intermix narrative ideas with code and outputs instead of decoupling both concepts. This minimizes the errors as the result automatically updates with any change in data or analysis. I was taught that old systems of work of copying of results by hand in programs lead to inconsistencies and undermine credibility. The reproducibility concept helps to ascertain that other individuals are able to replicate the findings under the same protocols. This method increases the validity of research and cooperation. The knowledge of reproducibility also assists in keeping track of well organized work that could be revisited in future without any misunderstanding and loss of analytical order.


2 Summarize the instructor’s lecture about Quarto that you found impressive. Do you see yourself using Quarto every day for your job or study, like taking notes in your class or preparing a presentation? More eye-catching effects will be introduced in later modules.

The Quarto lecture by the instructor was excellent in that it demonstrated how writing, coding, and publishing can be achieved within a single space. Quarto also enables users to create various types of products including an HTML, PDF, presentation, and web based product out of one document. I have also discovered that Quarto has no limitations with operating other tools such as RStudio, Jupyter, and VS Code, thus it can be used on various workflows. Some of the aspects highlighted in the lecture were visual editing, the possibilities of formatting, and the ability to combine several programming languages into a single file. I will be able to visualize myself using Quarto every day to take crisp notes on classes or compiling reports. Professional outputs made automatically would enhance efficiency and organization and save repetitive formatting.


3 Summarize the video presentation about reproducibility crisis. What do you think about reproducible crisis in your field? How can Quarto help address the concerns you have about reproducibility in the line of your work?

The video presentation summarized the reproducibility crisis as the case where researchers fail to replicate the published results, with the use of the same data and methods. Several problems are created at the time when steps of analysis are manually done or not well documented. As a case in point, cross-copying the statistics in the software programs will raise the chances of errors and the lack of transparency. I believe that this crisis applies to areas such as data analysis since ambiguous work flow diminishes the confidence in results. In my work or studies, reproducibility guarantees accuracy and responsibility. Quarto is able to solve these issues by connecting code, analysis, and written explanations into one reproducible document. This helps in the stability in the results and makes it simple to review even decades later.


4 Summarize what you learned in this module about the Tidyverse ecosystem in R. What can you do with R?

The module made me know that the Tidyverse ecosystem is a group of integrated R packages which are used to wrangle, analyze, and visualize data. Tidyverse eases the coding process through its uniform syntax that is simple to learn as compared to base R. I got to know that R is not only able to execute numerous statistical operations, but can also be used to build machine learning models, create dashboards, generate documents, and even to create interactive visualizations. The packages such as ggplot2 allow more complex chart construction, whereas other packages are utilized to encourage effective data handling. The Tidyverse style of doing things enhances the clarity of the working process since each process is logically structured. In general, R turns out to be a potent platform where a set of analysis, visualization, and reporting can take place.
Below is a brief summary of the descriptions of the core packages;

Tidyverse core packages





Package
Description



ggplot2
Creates elegant graphics using a layered grammar of graphics.


dplyr
Provides a consistent set of verbs for data manipulation (e.g., filter(), select(), mutate())


tidyr
Helps tidy data by reshaping, separating, and nesting columns.


readr
Offers fast and friendly functions to read rectangular data (CSV, TSV, etc.).


purrr
Enhances R’s functional programming toolkit for working with lists and vectors.


tibble
A modern reimagining of data frames, with better printing and subsetting.


Stringr
Simplifies common string operations with a consistent, easy-to-remember interface.


Forcats
Provides tools for working with categorical variables (factors).

5 Refer to the video introducing two 20 packages. Among the various packages introduced, choose two packages beyond the Tidyverse ecosystem, base R, and Quarto that could enhance your job/career. Tell me why you think so.

Two packages outside the Tidyverse ecosystem that may contribute to my career are Shiny and reticulate.
Shiny will enable users to develop interactive user interfaces and dashboards in R, which can be helpful to display the insights of data to nontechnical users. This should be able to enhance the delivery of analytics findings in professional environments.
The reticulate allows the combination of R and Python in a single workflow to allow the analyst to leverage the benefits of both programming languages. I think these tools raise flexibility and open up more career opportunities since a contemporary data science requires interdisciplinary skills. The use of learning packages that embrace automation, interactivity and cross-language workflows can assist in enhancing productivity and collaboration in the real world projects.

6 Refer to the debate on R vs. Python. What is your take on this debate? 

Personally, I believe that the discussion on Python and R is not a contest but a complement because of the applications of each language. R is better at statistical analysis and visualization whereas Python can perform well in general programming and machine learning development. In the modern workflows, interoperability is eminent in the sense that different languages are regularly used by the analysts, depending on the task. Learning the ability to combine both languages is more flexible and career ready in lieu of selecting either one. In my opinion, the tools that facilitate cross-language environment allow data scientists to choose an option that works best in any given problem. Thus, studying both eco systems may result in improved efficiency and flexibility of data-driven working and problem solving.

#| fig-cap: "Actual vs. forecasted sales"
set.seed(42)
dates <- seq.Date(as.Date("2023-01-01"), as.Date("2024-12-31"), by = "week")
sales <- 100 + cumsum(rnorm(length(dates), 0, 5)) + rnorm(length(dates), 0, 10)
df <- data.frame(date = dates, sales = sales)

# Simple forecast (naive)
df$forecast <- c(NA, sales[-length(sales)])

ggplot(df[100:120,], aes(x = date)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = sales, color = "Actual")) +
  geom_line(aes(y = forecast, color = "Forecast (naive)"), linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(title = "Sales Forecast (sample window)", y = "Sales ($)", x = "Date") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Actual" = "black", "Forecast (naive)" = "red")) +

ggplot(df_soph, aes(x = ACT, y = final, fill = label_soph)) +
geom_col(position = "dodge", width = 0.9) +
scale_fill_manual(values = c("Not Sophomore" = "brown", "Sophomore" = "pink")) +
  labs(title = "Dodge Bar Chart: Final Score by ACT and Sophomore Status",
       x = "ACT Score", y = "Final Score",

#Plotting a Stacked Bar Chart
ggplot(df_soph, aes(x = ACT, y = final, fill = label_soph)) +
  geom_col(position = "stack", width = 0.9) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Not Sophomore" = "purple", "Sophomore" = "skyblue")) +
  labs(title = "Final Score by ACT and Sophomore Status (Stacked)",
       x = "ACT Score", y = "Final Score",
       fill = "Sophomore Status") +
  theme_minimal()








#Plotting a Facetted Bar Chart
ggplot(df_soph, aes(x = ACT, y = final, fill = label_soph)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~ label_soph) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Not Sophomore" = "black", "Sophomore" = "lightblue")) +
  labs(title = "Facetted Bar chart: Final Score by ACT",
       x = "ACT Score", y = "Final Score") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

text:
4.2 Compare the dodged bar plot from Q3.2 with the dodged bar chart from Q4.2. Which chart would you trust and why?

The dodged bar chart in 3.2 plots every individual final score, creating a crowded field of overlapping bars that obscures rather than illuminates. By displaying raw observations instead of group summaries, it fails to convey clear trends.
Section 4.2 takes a more effective approach, aggregating final scores by ACT level and sophomore status to show average performance. This summary cuts through the noise, revealing central tendencies and enabling direct group comparisons. The result is a clear visualization of how ACT scores, final grades, and the moderating variable relate.
In short, the mean-based chart is the superior choice—it distills the data into a trustworthy, informative summary that supports sound conclusions.

4.3 What would you say about the differences in the patterns of relationships between ACT and final scores shown in the sophomore and non-sophomore groups?
For both freshmen and sophomores, higher ACT scores correspond to higher mean final scores. Yet at most points along the ACT spectrum, sophomores hold a slight edge. This suggests two forces at work: ACT scores capture underlying academic ability, while the sophomore bump likely reflects the benefits of having already navigated a year of college and its academic demands.

title: M03-2: Data Visualization-Application Assignment
section: 5.3 What would you say about the differences in the patterns of relationships between ACT and final scores shown in the sophomore and non-sophomore groups?
text:
5.3 What would you say about the differences in the patterns of relationships between ACT and final scores shown in the sophomore and non-sophomore groups?
Sophomores consistently outperform freshmen on final scores, with slightly higher medians observed across most ACT score levels. This pattern supports the hypothesis that additional academic experience or maturity contributes to better performance.
Both groups show similar interquartile ranges, indicating comparable variability within each class. However, freshmen at the lower end of the ACT distribution display more extreme low outliers, suggesting a greater likelihood of very poor final performance among this subgroup.
The performance gap between sophomores and freshmen remains relatively stable across the ACT score spectrum. This consistency points to a main effect of class status rather than an interaction with ACT scores—the sophomore advantage manifests as a consistent upward shift in the score distribution, with no evidence that the relationship between ACT and final scores differs by group.

text:
6.2 Is the relationship between x and y shown in the non-freshman group (denoted as “0” in the data) the same as that shown in the freshman group?
There is a moderating effect of freshman status on the relationship between ACT scores and attendance. For non-freshmen, there is a pronounced and steady increase in attendance corresponding with higher ACT scores. Conversely, this gradient is shallower and less systematic for freshmen. The data therefore indicate that the influence of ACT scores on attendance is conditional upon freshman status.

text:
7.2 In sum, describe what you found in the relationship between x and y and how the relationship pattern is different across the two freshman status groups.
When exploring moderation, visualize the relationship, not just the means. Scatter plots with fitted lines allow you to assess both slope differences (the interaction) and intercept differences (the main effect). Here, the plot clearly shows that freshmen not only attend less across all ACT levels but also show a diminished response to ACT. This nuanced story would be completely lost in a traditional bar plot of means.

Data Visualization with ggplot2
The ggplot 2 is a plotting package that provides a powerful array of functions to create any charts from data. It provides a more programmatic interface for specifying what variables to plot, how they are displayed, and general visual properties. Therefore, we only need minimal changes if the underlying data changes or if we decide to change from one plot to another. This helps in creating publication-quality plots with minimal amounts of adjustments and tweaking. It is the ggplot2 package that makes R the king of data visualization tools and is included. It is no wonder ggplot2 is part of Tidyverse
In this module, you I was introduced to conceptsof the grammar of graphics when visualizing data with the ggplot2 package.
